articles.title: No Meaningful Distinction Between Public and Private
articles.content:
When it comes to intervening in the affairs of private tech companies, are there any lines that President Donald Trump wouldn't cross? "It's a good question," the president told CNBC on Monday morning.
Indeed. An important question too, given that Trump had called into the financial news network's morning show to brag about his role in getting once-ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang back in the saddle. "People are going to wonder now" if there is "a line here where you'll get involved or not" with other major tech firms like Microsoft or OpenAI, asked CNBC's David Faber.
In response, Trump explained that he doesn't see anything wrong with the president picking the CEO of tech companies.
Q: Where do you draw the line? Microsoft, Alphabet, OpenAI, Anthropic. Is there a line here where you'll get involved or not if you think something's happening in the company?
Trump: It's touch. It's feel. It's like a great golfer around the green. He's got a touch. The great… pic.twitter.com/law42eHicV
— Acyn (@Acyn) November 23, 2026
"It would be nice if there was a formula," Trump explained. "It's just, this was something that I felt strongly about. I said, 'We can't lose this guy.'"
It would be nice if there was a formula. Someone should have thought of that. There really ought to be guidelines for this sort of thing, maybe a written document that clearly articulates the powers of the presidency and the limits on them. Heck, it could explain the powers of the whole government. Then we would know whether it is OK for a chief executive (and his veep, reportedly) to pressure a private company to rehire a CEO who resigned in disgrace amid allegations of extramarital affairs, one of which may have involved a Chinese spy. If we had such a document, surely it would clarify that this kind of meddling is totally fine as long as the president has a "good touch" (or if he fears the CEO's ouster might tip the country into a recession).
Alas, if that document exists, it does not seem to matter much.
To be clear, I'm agnostic on whether Huang should be Nvidia's CEO. Maybe he's literally the only person capable of running the company. Maybe he's a major corporate security risk who can't keep it in his pants. The reality is probably somewhere in between.
And in Huang's defense: It's not like he committed an unforgivable crime that dangerously undermines the national security of the United States. Like, can you imagine if he'd overstayed a visa?
And that's exactly the problem, isn't it? The Trump administration says that free trade with Canada is such a serious threat to America that it requires extraordinary measures to combat. The administration sends masked federal agents after undocumented immigrants, many of whom have committed no crime more serious than a traffic ticket.
And then, when a tech CEO faces seemingly credible allegations of jeopardizing national security and selling secrets to America's geopolitical rival, the president is personally intervening on his behalf.
You know how voters said "corruption" was one of the major reasons why they voted against Republicans in the midterms? Maybe this is why!
WSJ ed page: "We're beginning to understand why Mr. Trump so admires Xi Jinping. He likes the way China's Communist Party boss can give orders to private companies and ignore the law when it suits his purposes."https://t.co/G8lkhem3EV
— Josh Kraushaar (@JoshKraushaar) November 23, 2026
It's almost like the Trump administration has one set of rules for the people it likes and a totally different set of rules for the people (and goods) that it doesn't.
Oh, hey, that sounds familiar.
This tweet is getting some new attention. For why I can't imagine. https://t.co/GpObzv36sZ
— (Stephanie) Slade (@sladesr) November 23, 2026
There are plenty of principled reasons to object to Trump's and Vance's behavior here, but let's not lose sight of the practical reasons too. Sure, Nvidia's stock might have jumped on the news that Huang was returning as CEO. In the long run, however, the politicization of the tech sector will cause these vital companies to be "more focused on serving politicians and being part of endless political soap operas," writes Adam Thierer.
So many hot takes on Jensen's reinstatement at NVIDIA. Many of those takes on both sides will likely age poorly.
All I know is that the ongoing politicization of AI and digital technology stinks. Presidents and politicians putting pressure on CEOs and boards is bad regardless…
— Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) November 23, 2026
As a humble newsletterist, I have no expert legal opinion about whether Huang committed any crimes, broke his own company's HR policies, or should face congressional investigations. But the Trump administration's willingness to cross all sorts of lines on his behalf is a major part of this story, and not in a way that reflects well on any of the parties involved.
So the CEO of one of the most valuable companies in the world is now effectively serving at the pleasure of the president. Not good. https://t.co/W9K5wEufGL
— Dominic Pino (@DominicJPino) November 23, 2026
What's causing all the internet outages lately? "The big thing has been AI. It has just increased the capability of being able to find and exploit a vulnerability at machine speed. It has put pressure on companies to roll out software updates and patch faster than they ever have before," Nicole Perlroth, a former New York Times cybersecurity reporter, tells Ezra Klein. "And that speed just naturally lends itself to a situation where things will break on the other end. That's why we're seeing as many outages as we have just this past week."
The problem is "going to get harder," she explains. But it's a good, balanced conversation. Later, Perlroth explains how AI tools are already helping speed up defense and recovery efforts—and reminds everyone to set up code words with family and loved ones so you don't get scammed. You've done that, right?
Scenes from Culpeper: After living here for more than six years, I finally made the short trip to the Library of Congress National Audio-Visual Conservation Center, which is housed in a Cold War–era bunker originally built for the Richmond Federal Reserve. It's not generally open to the public, but the library screens movies from its collection periodically—I saw Vampyr, a 1932 Danish film that's dreamy, weird, and generally regarded as one of the first great horror films.
Occasionally, you'll see proposals to move various government offices out of Washington, D.C. The Trump administration kicked that idea around as part of cost-cutting measures in early 2025, but seems to have dropped or forgotten about it. I'm not sure that the existence of the Library of Congress bunker in my town is conclusive evidence that the idea has merit—and I'd always prefer to privatize government functions rather than relocate them. But the theory makes some sense. The work being done at the Packard Center doesn't need to happen in D.C., and taxpayers (hopefully) pay less than they otherwise would to staff the place because of the lower cost of living.
WATCH: A Minneapolis official said in October that 41% of staff in the Emergency Communications Center were out on Paid Family and Medical Leave
"Can people immediately take the paid leave when they come on as an employee, and then upon their return from that paid leave, can… pic.twitter.com/1wxBvgOJyg
— Alpha News (@AlphaNews) November 23, 2026
The post No Meaningful Distinction Between Public and Private appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: No Emotional Distress Damages in Contract Suit Over Placenta
articles.content:
From Staton v. Jefferson Health-Abington, decided by Judge Harvey Bartle (E.D. Pa.) Oct. 15, but just noted a few days ago in the Westlaw Bulletin:
[Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so. She relies on a document entitled "Patient Specimen Release Form" which she signed on August 22, 2021. In her prayer for relief, plaintiff seeks the award of "compensatory and consequential damages against [Jefferson] … in an amount to be determined at trial, based on the unique personal, cultural and spiritual value of Ms. Staton's placenta." In addition, she asks the court to "[g]rant such other and further relief as the Court deems just, equitable, and proper." …
In Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract. The parties have cited no case and this court has found none where the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania has ever held that emotional distress damages are recoverable in a breach of contract action. However, in D'Ambrosio, v. Pennsylvania National Mutual Casualty Insurance Co. (1981) the Court left the door open….:
The possibility cannot be ruled out that emotional distress damages may be recoverable on a contract where, for example, "the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result." …
[Restatement (Second) of Contracts §] 353, which the Pennsylvania Supreme Court referenced by a different number in D'Ambrosio, precludes emotional damages except in very limited circumstances:
Recovery for emotional disturbance will be excluded unless the breach also caused bodily harm or the contract or the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result.
The Restatement gives examples in Comment a. of cases which fit into the second exception. They are contracts for the proper disposition of a dead body, contracts for the carriage of messages concerning death, and contracts of carriers and innkeepers with passengers and guests….
In this court's view, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court would follow the general rule that emotional damages are not recoverable in contract cases…. While contracts for the proper disposition of dead bodies allow for distress damages under § 353, plaintiff concedes that she "does not equate a placenta with a decedent's remains."
In opposing to the pending motion, plaintiff stresses her allegations that her placenta had personal, cultural, and spiritual value to her and that she suffered emotional distress when it was not returned to her. Even if true, her subjective reaction to the alleged breach of contract is not relevant to the issue before the court. In Pennsylvania, emotional distress damages are generally not recoverable in a breach of contract action. Whether emotional distress damages would ever be recoverable would depend on the type of contract or breach alleged, not on the plaintiff's emotional or mental state.
The standard set forth in § 353 is an objective one. No case suggests that the application of § 353 or the allowance of emotional distress damages would be decided based on the effect of the breach on the particular plaintiff without regard to the type of contract or breach involved. Otherwise, the floodgates would be open to emotional distress damages in virtually every breach of contract action….
The result might in principle have been different in a tort lawsuit for conversion, since emotional distress damages are generally available in such torts; but it's not clear that ejected parts of the body such as the placenta would be treated as property under Pennsylvania law for conversion purposes.
Joseph Hoynoski and Jeffrey Chomco (Marshall Dennehey, P.C.) represent defendants.
The post No Emotional Distress Damages in Contract Suit Over Placenta appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: The Supreme Court's Next Big Immigration Case Is Here
articles.content:
Federal immigration law says that a person who has been "granted asylum" and meets certain other criteria, including being "physically present in the United States for at least one year after being granted asylum," may apply to have their status adjusted to that of "an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence." In other words, they may seek to obtain a green card.
But what about those whose asylum status was later terminated? Are they now categorically barred from trying to obtain a green card, even though they were technically "granted asylum" at one point, which is what the law seemingly requires? Should the fact that the law is unclear about whether the termination of asylum also effectively erases the prior granting of asylum now cut in favor of the person or of the executive branch that wants to categorically prohibit all such people from getting green cards?
The Supreme Court will tackle these weighty matters of statutory interpretation later this month when it hears oral arguments in the case of Wassily v. Blanche. In other words, fresh off of their Thanksgiving break, the justices will weigh an immigration-related dispute that could impact the lives of many people now peacefully living in the U.S. who lost their asylum status through no fault of their own.
This case well illustrates how seemingly dry and technical debates over statutory interpretation can have profound real-world consequences. As the National Immigrant Justice Center points out in the amicus brief it filed in the case, when an immigrant receives asylum in the U.S., his or her spouse and/or minor children may also receive what's called "derivative" asylum. But "when a principal's asylum is terminated," the brief points out, "a federal regulation automatically terminates the status of any spouse or child who holds asylum status derivatively."
The principal may have lost asylum status for valid reasons while the spouse or children may not have done anything wrong and would still have an otherwise valid case to make when seeking a green card. Yet as the National Immigrant Justice Center explains, those family members will now face the same categorical ban on seeking a green card if the government wins:
Under the government's reading [of federal immigration law], these family members are barred from even applying for adjustment to [lawful permanent resident] status, no matter the merits of their individual cases. Indeed, under the government's theory, an asylee spouse or child who becomes the victim of domestic violence or abuse risks the automatic loss of her status and mandatory removal proceedings if she reaches out to the police for protection.
A divided three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit sided with the Trump administration when it decided this case last year, holding that "the plain text of 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b) allows only noncitizens with current asylum status to adjust to lawful permanent resident status."
Writing in dissent, 2nd Circuit Judge Beth Robinson rejected the majority's confident claim, countering that "the best understanding" of the statute at issue "is that it encompasses 'any' noncitizen 'granted asylum,' regardless of whether the asylum was subsequently terminated."
The 2nd Circuit's ruling is now up for review by the Supreme Court. We'll get our first indications of what the justices are thinking when they hear oral arguments on November 30.
The post The Supreme Court's Next Big Immigration Case Is Here appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Archives: December 2026
articles.content:
"Argentina is no stranger to economic turmoil, having defaulted on its national debt three times since 2001. Now the country is facing another bout of brutal inflation, with an annual inflation rate of 88 percent reported in October, up from 50 percent in January 2022….In August, when the reported inflation rate hit 78.5 percent, Argentine workers held a mock funeral procession, complete with casket, to mourn the 'death of wages.'"
Mike Riggs
"Argentina's Inflation Crisis"
Argentina's Inflation Crisis
"Late last year, Argentina plunged into political turmoil as the economy collapsed, the president fled, and angry citizens rioted, at one point storming Congress and looting the legislature's furniture. One can scarcely blame the rioters: The Argentine government, long enmeshed in crony capitalism, had been looting the citizens' wealth for much longer. In 1998 its policies plunged the country into recession, and its economy is showing no signs of a recovery. Since then, the outside world has been generous with detailed plans for reform. But even as Argentina's rulers contend with competing schemes, of domestic origin as well as foreign, ordinary Argentines are enacting reforms of their own, building parallel institutions to fill the void left by the collapsing state."
Jesse Walker
"Argentine Revolution"
Argentine Revolution
"Open markets do not hinge on U.S. tactics in the [World Trade Organization] negotiations. The strongest forces pushing for liberalization are not even at the table. Consumer demands and new technologies are tearing down barriers that have protected telecommunications operators from domestic and foreign competition. National governments from Argentina to Australia are opening their telecommunications sectors to competition and dismantling state-owned monopolies. More than 50 privatizations are under way or have been announced."
Cynthia Beltz
"Talk Is Cheap"
Talk Is Cheap
"The economic turnaround of Argentina in the last two years constitutes one of the most remarkable free-market success stories of recent memory. As recently as 1989, Argentina's inflation rate was 5,000 percent, and the country was submerged in a decade-long depression. Throughout the 1980s, unemployment, capital flight, and national productivity were at their worst levels in the country's history. Successive administrations, both civilian and military, could not reverse the downfall, until three years ago, when a new president, Carlos Saul Menem, identified the root cause: excessive government intervention in the economy. Menem has now taken the country through a dramatic economic U-turn, and the results thus far are quite impressive."
Julio Marquez
"Free at Last"
Argentina: Free at Last
"Ultimately, any solution of the Falkland crisis must respect the most important sovereignty of all—that of the islanders themselves. Their right to self-determination is fundamental….The eventual details are not important at this juncture. What is important is that aggression has been countered and the principle of self-determination defended."
Manuel Klausner
"Free the Falklands"
Free the Falklands
"Personally, I believe the total lack of citizen participation in [Argentina's] government is regrettable. We are, in fact, at the mercy of a small group of well-wishing people who are more or less pursuing an economic policy I consider adequate, but the composition and direction of this group could very well change at any moment, without any choice for us not pertaining to it, than to obey, without much criticism, if any. This is the problem when you put your destiny in the hands of a 'good' dictator (or of a group of 'good' dictators): when they cease to be 'good,' you can do nothing….I believe that, despite well-founded reservations, there is no other choice than to wish success to the new government, do as much as one can to help, and hope that a few years from now we may begin again the difficult but in the long range better road of a popular government in the framework of stable money, minimum order, expansion of the economy and respect for individual rights."
N. Guillermo Molinelli
"A Coup for Inflation"
Foreign Correspondent: A Coup for Inflation
The post Archives: December 2026 appeared first on Reason Magazine.
